subsystems.name: DNA design software
subsystems.role: turns a desired function into a DNA sequence that a cell can read.
parts: genetic-part libraries (promoters, ribosome binding sites, terminators)

subsystems.name: DNA synthesis and assembly
subsystems.role: builds the designed sequence physically as double-stranded DNA.
parts: assembly methods that join fragments into genes and multi-gene constructs

subsystems.name: Chassis and genome editing
subsystems.role: the host cell that will run the new instructions.
parts: microbial hosts such as bacteria and yeast, plus mammalian cell lines

subsystems.name: Expression control
subsystems.role: keeps each gene switched to the right level at the right time.
parts: biosensors that report on internal state

subsystems.name: Test and measurement
subsystems.role: measures what the engineered cells actually do, far faster than a human can.
parts: automated liquid handling and colony picking
mass spectrometry and other analytical instruments

subsystems.name: Scale-up bioprocessing
subsystems.role: grows the engineered organism at industrial volume and recovers the product.

buildSteps.title: Define the specification
buildSteps.detail: State precisely what the organism must make or sense, at what yield, in what conditions, and what it must not do.

buildSteps.title: Design the genetic programme
buildSteps.detail: Choose host and parts, model the metabolic pathway, and write out a DNA sequence predicted to work.

buildSteps.title: Synthesise the DNA
buildSteps.detail: Order or build the gene constructs chemically, then verify every base by sequencing before use.

buildSteps.title: Transform or edit the host
buildSteps.detail: Introduce the construct, or edit the existing genome, so the cell carries the new instructions.

buildSteps.title: Screen variants
buildSteps.detail: Grow many colonies in parallel, test each for output, and keep the best performers.

buildSteps.title: Iterate the design–build–test–learn cycle
buildSteps.detail: Feed the measurements back into the model and redesign; this loop repeats many times and is the core of the field.

buildSteps.title: Scale up fermentation
buildSteps.detail: Move the winning strain into progressively larger bioreactors, tuning oxygen, temperature, pH and feed. Evolution and contamination are the main risks.

buildSteps.title: Purify and formulate
buildSteps.detail: Separate the product from cells and broth, then test it against the specification and regulatory standards.

buildSteps.title: Add biocontainment
buildSteps.detail: Where required, engineer dependence on a nutrient the organism cannot find in the wild, so it cannot survive an accidental release.

prerequisites.why: you cannot engineer what you cannot read, and design cycles depend on fast verification.
short constructs are routine and cheap; long, error-free DNA and whole genomes remain difficult and costly.
CRISPR-based tools let engineers change a chosen site in a genome rather than random mutagenesis.
biology is noisy and context-dependent, so most designs still need many trial-and-error rounds.
robots and software compress the cycle from months to days, but few facilities are fully integrated.
proven in antibiotics and industrial enzymes; adapting it to new molecules is often the real bottleneck.

pathway.milestone: engineered microbes already make recombinant insulin, industrial enzymes, vitamins and a antimalarial drug precursor
pathway.unlocks: a commercial base and regulatory precedent for further products.

pathway.milestone: standardised, well-characterised parts and reliable computer-aided design
pathway.unlocks: first-attempt designs that work, cutting the trial-and-error cost.
faster production without the constraint of keeping cells alive.

pathway.milestone: engineered cells and tissues for medicine and materials
pathway.unlocks: living therapies, sustainable chemicals and substitutes for petrochemical products — provided biocontainment and governance keep pace.
